**Slides covered.** `BIOS-767-Part-002.pdf`, slides 8-46; `BIOS-767-Part-003.pdf`, slides 4-31; `BIOS-767-Part-007.pdf`, slides 21-71; `Lecture-07-Part2.pdf`, document pp. 1-12; `REML derivation.pdf`, document pp. 1-8.

## Motivation

Longitudinal analysis is multivariate analysis with scientifically ordered components. Valid estimation must account for unequal marginal variances and within-subject covariance. The multivariate normal model supplies a full likelihood for continuous outcomes; GLS/WLS supplies moment-based estimation when a complete distribution is unnecessary.

## Multivariate normal model

For $Y\in\mathbb R^n$,

$$
Y\sim N_n(\mu,\Sigma),\qquad
f(y)=\frac{\exp\{-\tfrac12(y-\mu)^\mathsf T\Sigma^{-1}(y-\mu)\}}
{(2\pi)^{n/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}},
$$

where $\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(Y)$ is symmetric positive definite. Writing $T=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{11},\ldots,\sigma_{nn})$ and $R=\operatorname{Corr}(Y)$,

$$
\Sigma=T^{1/2}RT^{1/2}.
$$

Positive definiteness is required for a nonsingular density and implies $c^\mathsf T\Sigma c>0$ for all $c\ne0$. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-002.pdf`, slides 9-13 and 23-24.*

For a fixed $r\times n$ matrix $A$ and vector $a$,

$$
AY+a\sim N_r(A\mu+a,A\Sigma A^\mathsf T).
$$

Thus contrasts, changes from baseline, and linear summaries remain normal. If

$$
Y=\begin{pmatrix}Y_1\\Y_2\end{pmatrix},\quad
\mu=\begin{pmatrix}\mu_1\\\mu_2\end{pmatrix},\quad
\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{11}&\Sigma_{12}\\\Sigma_{21}&\Sigma_{22}\end{pmatrix},
$$

then

$$
Y_1\mid Y_2=y_2\sim N\!\left(
\mu_1+\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(y_2-\mu_2),
\Sigma_{11}-\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}
\right).
$$

The transformation proof is assigned on `BIOS-767-Part-002.pdf`, slide 38; the conditional-normal result and example are on slides 43-44.

The squared Mahalanobis distance

$$
D^2=(Y-\mu)^\mathsf T\Sigma^{-1}(Y-\mu)
$$

has a $\chi_n^2$ distribution under the model. Its empirical version is a cluster-level outlier measure, not a collection of independent univariate residual tests. The whitening proof appears on `BIOS-767-Part-002.pdf`, slide 42.

## Gaussian longitudinal mean model

For independent subjects,

$$
Y_i\sim N_{n_i}\{X_i\beta,\Sigma_i(\theta)\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.
$$

The design $X_i$ may contain treatment, categorical visit, continuous time, interactions, polynomials, or spline bases. The covariance dimension may vary with $n_i$. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-007.pdf`, slides 6-8.*

The log-likelihood, up to a constant, is

$$
\ell(\beta,\theta)
=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N
\left[
\log|\Sigma_i(\theta)|
+\{Y_i-X_i\beta\}^\mathsf T\Sigma_i(\theta)^{-1}\{Y_i-X_i\beta\}
\right].
$$

Conditional on $\theta$, the GLS estimator is

$$
\widehat\beta(\theta)=
\left(\sum_iX_i^\mathsf T\Sigma_i^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}
\left(\sum_iX_i^\mathsf T\Sigma_i^{-1}Y_i\right),
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\{\widehat\beta(\theta)\}
=\left(\sum_iX_i^\mathsf T\Sigma_i^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}.
$$

ML alternates between estimating $\beta$ and covariance parameters because each estimator depends on the other. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-007.pdf`, slides 22-27.*

## WLS estimation of $\beta$ without a full distribution

WLS targets the mean-model parameter $\beta$. Assume only

$$
E(Y_i)=X_i\beta,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\Sigma_i,
$$

and let $W_i$ be fixed positive-definite weights. WLS minimizes

$$
Q_W(\beta)=\sum_i(Y_i-X_i\beta)^\mathsf TW_i(Y_i-X_i\beta)
$$

and gives

$$
\widehat\beta_W=
\left(\sum_iX_i^\mathsf TW_iX_i\right)^{-1}
\sum_iX_i^\mathsf TW_iY_i.
$$

If the mean model is correct and the weights are fixed, $E(\widehat\beta_W)=\beta$ for any $W_i$. The choice $W_i=\Sigma_i^{-1}$ is efficient within the WLS class. Working independence $W_i=I$ preserves unbiased point estimation but invalidates an independence-based variance estimator. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-007.pdf`, slides 33-39; `Lecture-07-Part2.pdf`, document pp. 4-7.*

Define

$$
B=\sum_iX_i^\mathsf TW_iX_i,\qquad
M=\sum_iX_i^\mathsf TW_i
(Y_i-X_i\widehat\beta_W)(Y_i-X_i\widehat\beta_W)^\mathsf T
W_iX_i.
$$

The cluster-robust covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\mathrm{rob}}(\widehat\beta_W)
=B^{-1}MB^{-1}.
$$

It remains consistent under covariance misspecification, provided clusters are independent, the mean is correct, regularity conditions hold, and $N$ is sufficiently large. It does not protect against a misspecified mean. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-007.pdf`, slides 55-59 and 64-67.*

## ML versus REML for covariance estimation

For $Y\sim N_n(X\beta,V_\theta)$, let $\theta$ parameterize the covariance structure and let $p=\operatorname{rank}(X)$. Both ML and REML are used to estimate $\theta$; after obtaining $\widehat\theta$, the fixed effects are estimated by GLS,

$$
\widehat\beta(\widehat\theta)
=
\left(X^\mathsf TV_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}X\right)^{-1}
X^\mathsf TV_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}Y.
$$

ML jointly maximizes $\ell(\beta,\theta)$ over $(\beta,\theta)$. Equivalently, profiling out $\beta$ gives

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{ML}}(\theta)
=-\frac12\left[
\log|V_\theta|
+(Y-X\widehat\beta_\theta)^\mathsf TV_\theta^{-1}(Y-X\widehat\beta_\theta)
\right]+C.
$$

REML instead constructs a likelihood for $\theta$ from $n-p$ linearly independent error contrasts $A^\mathsf TY$ satisfying $A^\mathsf TX=0$. Since

$$
A^\mathsf TY=A^\mathsf T\varepsilon
\sim N_{n-p}(0,A^\mathsf TV_\theta A),
$$

this likelihood contains $\theta$ but not $\beta$. Equivalently, REML can be derived by integrating the Gaussian likelihood over $\beta$ with respect to a flat measure; it does not mean that $\beta$ is absent from the fitted model. The resulting criterion is

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{REML}}(\theta)
=-\frac12\left[
\log|V_\theta|
+\log|X^\mathsf TV_\theta^{-1}X|
+(Y-X\widehat\beta_\theta)^\mathsf TV_\theta^{-1}(Y-X\widehat\beta_\theta)
\right]+C_X.
$$

Thus ML estimates $\beta$ and $\theta$ from the full likelihood without a residual degrees-of-freedom correction, whereas REML estimates $\theta$ from the portion of $Y$ orthogonal to the fixed-effect space. The REML adjustment accounts for estimating $p$ fixed-effect parameters and usually reduces small-sample bias in covariance estimation. In the iid normal model, ML divides the residual sum of squares by $n$, whereas REML divides by $n-p$. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-003.pdf`, slides 15-18 and 24-31.*

### Implication for choosing ML or REML

The restricted likelihood is defined from the residual subspace $\mathcal C(X)^\perp$. Changing $X$ changes the error contrasts and therefore changes the restricted likelihood being evaluated. For valid likelihood-based model comparison, use the following rules:

- To compare fixed-effect mean models $X_0$ and $X_1$, fit both by ML using the same covariance-model family $V_\theta$; estimate $\theta$ separately under each mean model.
- To compare covariance structures $V_{\theta,0}$ and $V_{\theta,1}$ by REML, use the same fixed-effect design $X$ in both models.
- After selecting the mean and covariance structures, refit by REML to estimate $\theta$, then estimate $\beta$ by GLS using $V_{\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{REML}}}$.

*Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-003.pdf`, slides 29-31; `BIOS-767-Part-009.pdf`, slides 80-88 and 111-123.*

## Inference

For $H_0:C\beta=c$, the large-sample Wald statistic is

$$
W=(C\widehat\beta-c)^\mathsf T
\{C\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\beta)C^\mathsf T\}^{-1}
(C\widehat\beta-c)
\ \dot\sim\ \chi_r^2,\qquad r=\operatorname{rank}(C).
$$

For nested likelihood models,

$$
G^2=2\{\ell_{\mathrm{full}}-\ell_{\mathrm{reduced}}\}
\ \dot\sim\ \chi_{\Delta p}^2,
$$

when the null is interior and regularity conditions hold. Boundary nulls require nonstandard reference distributions. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-007.pdf`, slides 60-63.*

## Interpretation and when to apply

- Use the MVN likelihood when a continuous response is plausibly jointly Gaussian and likelihood-based MAR inference or covariance modeling is important.
- Use WLS/GEE with a sandwich covariance when the marginal mean is primary and distributional robustness is preferred.
- Interpret $c^\mathsf T\beta$ as the adjusted mean contrast encoded by $c$, conditional on the chosen design and time origin.
- Interpret covariance parameters only under the specified covariance family; a working covariance in GEE is primarily an efficiency device unless association is itself modeled.

## External cross-check

The GLS, likelihood, and error-contrast formulations agree with standard Gaussian linear-model theory; the LMM specialization is cross-checked against [Laird and Ware (1982)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7168798/).
